title: The good and the pleasant
theme: Death’s teaching begins: the good and the pleasant are different, both lay hold of a person, and the one who chooses the pleasant misses the goal.

words.gram: pres. participle middle, m. gen. sg.
words.role: the person for whom it goes well
verb of the main clause of the third sentence
subject of the relative clause; its correlative is the subject of हीयते

sandhi.type: t before ś; aḥ before a; t before a vowel; vṛddhi
sandhi.rule: anyat + śreyaḥ: t becomes c before ś, P. 8.4.40 (स्तोः श्चुना श्चुः), and the ś becomes ch, P. 8.4.63 (शश्छोऽटि). śreyaḥ before a: the visarga becomes u, P. 6.1.113 (अतो रोरप्लुतादप्लुते), a + u give o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः), and the a that follows is taken into the o, P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति) — the avagraha marks it. anyat before u: t becomes d, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते). uta + eva: a + e give ai, P. 6.1.88 (वृद्धिरेचि).

preyaḥ before t: the visarga becomes s, P. 8.3.34 (विसर्जनीयस्य सः). te is a dual ending in e and so pragṛhya, P. 1.1.11 (ईदूदेद्द्विवचनं प्रगृह्यम्): it does not combine with the u of ubhe, P. 6.1.125 (प्लुतप्रगृह्या अचि नित्यम्).
Final m before a consonant becomes anusvāra: P. 8.3.23 (मोऽनुस्वारः).

sandhi.type: aḥ before a vowel other than a
sandhi.rule: The visarga after a becomes y before a vowel, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), and the y is dropped, P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य). The hiatus that results is not joined again.

sandhi.type: e before a; t before a voiced sound; aḥ before u
sandhi.rule: hīyate + arthāt: the a is taken into the e, P. 6.1.109 (एङः पदान्तादति). arthāt before y: t becomes d, P. 8.2.39 (झलां जशोऽन्ते). yaḥ before u: the visarga becomes y and is dropped, P. 8.3.17 (भोभगोअघोअपूर्वस्य योऽशि), P. 8.3.19 (लोपः शाकल्यस्य).
The visarga becomes u before the voiced v, P. 6.1.114 (हशि च), and a + u give o, P. 6.1.87 (आद्गुणः).

sandhi_exceptions.note: te ubhe: the dual te is pragṛhya, P. 1.1.11 (ईदूदेद्द्विवचनं प्रगृह्यम्), and does not combine with the following vowel, P. 6.1.125 (प्लुतप्रगृह्या अचि नित्यम्).

samasa.meaning: the two whose aims are different; Śaṅkara: «भिन्नप्रयोजने»

morphology.note: Comparative in -īyas, P. 5.3.57 (द्विवचनविभज्योपपदे तरबीयसुनौ), of praśasya ‘praiseworthy’, which is replaced by śra- before it, P. 5.3.60 (प्रशस्यस्य श्रः): literally ‘the better’.

Comparative of priya ‘dear’, which becomes pra- before -īyas, P. 6.4.157 (प्रियस्थिरस्फिरोरुबहुलगुरुवृद्धतृप्रदीर्घवृन्दारकाणां प्रस्थस्फवर्बंहिगर्वर्षित्रब्द्राघिवृन्दाः): literally ‘the dearer’. The verse sets two comparatives against each other, not good against evil.
Present dual of si ‘bind’, ninth class (stem sinā-, weak sinī-). The two things ‘bind’ a person: they lay a claim on him.
Passive of hā ‘leave’: ‘is left’, ‘falls short’. With the ablative arthāt: ‘is deprived of the goal’.
Present participle middle of ā-dā ‘take [for oneself]’, in the genitive of the person concerned: ‘for the one taking [the good] it is well’.

translation.literal: ‘Other [is] the better, and quite other the dearer; these two, with different aims, bind a person. Of these two, it becomes good for the one taking the better; he falls away from the goal who just chooses the dearer.’
translation.readable: ‘The good is one thing, the pleasant quite another. Both, with their different ends, take hold of a person. It goes well with the one who takes the good; whoever chooses the pleasant misses the goal.’

anvaya: श्रेयः अन्यत्, उत प्रेयः एव अन्यत् । ते उभे नानार्थे [सती] पुरुषम् सिनीतः । तयोः श्रेयः आददानस्य साधु भवति । यः उ प्रेयः वृणीते [सः] अर्थात् हीयते ।
syntax: Three sentences. Two nominal clauses with the copula understood (anyac chreyaḥ, anyad … preyaḥ: ‘one thing is the good, another the pleasant’); a statement about both, with te ubhe as subject and sinītaḥ a dual verb; then a contrast: the genitive participle ādadānasya with sādhu bhavati (‘it goes well for the one taking’), and a relative clause, ya u preyo vṛṇīte, whose understood correlative is the subject of hīyate.

ambiguities.topic: In what sense do the two ‘bind’?
ambiguities.note: Śaṅkara: everyone who acts at all acts for one or the other, and so is said to be bound by both: «अतः श्रेयःप्रेयःप्रयोजनकर्तव्यतया ताभ्यां बद्ध इत्युच्यते सर्वः पुरुषः». Raṅgarāmānuja: they bring a person under their control, «पुरुषं स्ववशताम् आपादयतः इत्यर्थः».

The base, GRETIL, the vishvAsa mūla, Śaṅkara and Raṅgarāmānuja read uta eva, ‘and quite [other]’. Madhva’s text reads uteva, uta iva, ‘and as it were [other]’ (corrections.json). The base reading makes the difference absolute; Madhva’s would soften it, though his bhāṣya says nothing on the word.

metre.name: triṣṭubh
metre.note: The first half has the regular 22 syllables (11 + 11). The second half counts 25: the third pāda, tayoḥ śreya ādadānasya sādhu bhavati, has 14; the fourth, hīyate ’rthād ya u preyo vṛṇīte, the regular 11. The hiatuses śreya ā- and ya u are counted as written.

beginner: Death has tested Naciketas with every pleasure he could offer, and the boy has refused them all. Now Death begins to teach, and he starts with a choice everyone faces. There is what is good for us, and there is what is pleasant to us. They are not the same thing, and they pull in different directions; both have a hold on every person. Whoever takes the good does well. Whoever chooses the merely pleasant misses the real aim of life. The verse does not say that pleasure is wicked. It says that the pleasant and the good are two different things, and that a life is shaped by which of the two we allow to decide. Everything Death teaches afterwards rests on this first distinction.
analogy: Like two roads leaving a town by the same gate: one is pleasant to walk at first, the other goes where you actually need to arrive.

commentary.label: direct
commentary.text: That the good (śreyas) and the pleasant (preyas) are different, that both lay hold of a person, and that taking the good goes well while choosing the pleasant loses the goal. It is the first sentence of Death’s teaching, after the tests of 1.1.21–29.

commentary.q: Why does the teaching begin here?
commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: Śaṅkara: Death speaks having tested the pupil and found him fit for knowledge — «परीक्ष्य शिष्यं विद्यायोग्यतां चावगम्याह». The good is the highest good, «श्रेयः निःश्रेयसं»; the pleasant is ‘the dearer’, «प्रेयः प्रियतरमपि». The two are knowledge and ignorance, «ताभ्यां विद्याविद्याभ्याम्», and one person cannot pursue both together without giving one up: «अन्यतरापरित्यागेनैकेन पुरुषेण सहानुष्ठातुमशक्यत्वात्». The one who chooses the pleasant falls from the lasting aim: «प्रयोजनान्नित्यात् प्रच्यवत इत्यर्थः».

commentary.label: traditional
commentary.text: As Death’s praise of the desire for release, once he has tested the pupil and found that desire steady: «एवं शिष्यं परीक्ष्य, तस्य मुमुक्षा स्थैर्यं निश्चित्य». The good is the path of release, «अतिप्रशस्तं मोक्षवर्त्माऽपि अन्यत्»; the pleasant is the path of enjoyment, «प्रियत्वास्पदं भोगवर्त्मापि अन्यत्». Whoever chooses the pleasant falls from the human aim: «स पुरुषार्थाद्भ्रष्टो भवति».

commentary.q: What exactly are śreyas and preyas?
commentary.label: linguistic
commentary.text: Two comparatives in -īyas: śreyas of praśasya ‘praiseworthy’ (P. 5.3.60 (प्रशस्यस्य श्रः)), preyas of priya ‘dear’. Literally ‘the better’ and ‘the dearer’. Śaṅkara keeps the comparative in his gloss «प्रियतरमपि»: the pleasant is not bad, only dearer — preferred now.

advaita.text: The good is knowledge and the highest good; the pleasant is ignorance and worldly prosperity. Every person seeking prosperity or immortality acts for one of them: «प्रेयःश्रेयसोर्हि अभ्युदयामृतत्वार्थी पुरुषः प्रवर्तते». Since they are knowledge and ignorance, they exclude each other.

visistadvaita.text: The good is the path of release, the pleasant the path of enjoyment: «अतिप्रशस्तं मोक्षवर्त्माऽपि अन्यत्». The verse praises the pupil’s desire for release.

schools.disagreement: Both commentaries read the pair as the way to release against the way of enjoyment; Śaṅkara also identifies them with knowledge and ignorance, which cannot be combined. Madhva’s comment on the passage 1.2.1–3 is a single gloss on a word of 1.2.3; his text reads uteva for utaiva here.

parallels.note: The Gītā’s happiness of sattva is ‘like poison at first, like nectar in the end’. A thematic parallel: the Gītā draws the same line between what pleases now and what is good in the end.
The happiness that comes from the senses meeting their objects is the reverse: nectar at first, ‘like poison in the end’ — the Kaṭha’s preyas seen from its outcome.

contemporary.text: Much of what competes for attention today is designed to be preferred in the moment — the next video, the next notification. The verse’s word for it, preyas, is exactly that: ‘the more preferred’. It does not call it evil. It only observes that what we prefer now and what is good for us are different things, and that a life drifts toward whichever one is allowed to choose. This is a reflection on the teaching, not part of it.

reflect.beginner: Name one choice this week where the pleasant and the good pointed in different directions.
reflect.deeper: Is the good always unpleasant at first, or does the verse only say that the two are different?
reflect.practice: Before one ordinary decision today, ask plainly: which of these is the pleasant, and which the good?

flags.note: Madhva’s text reads uteva (uta iva) for utaiva (uta eva) (corrections.json).
Śaṅkara identifies śreyas and preyas with knowledge and ignorance; Raṅgarāmānuja with the paths of release and of enjoyment.
